notes.meaning: Jesus tells His disciples plainly that He must suffer, be rejected by the Jewish leaders, be killed, and rise on the third day. The elders, chief priests, and scribes made up the national council known as the Sanhedrin. His followers expected a king who would conquer earthly nations, but Jesus explained that His true path into His kingdom was through death and resurrection.

Jesus warns that anyone who wants to follow Him must say no to selfish desires and willingly bear suffering every day. In Roman times, a criminal carried his own crossbeam to his execution, so this means being ready for hardship and rejection. Believers should not go looking for trouble, but they must faithfully accept the trials God places in their path.

differ.view: This call to daily self-denial and cross-bearing is the basic gospel invitation showing how a sinner must surrender to Christ to be saved.
Taking up the cross daily is a strict duty for holy living, so that any day lived without bearing a cross for Christ is wasted.
This command describes a particular hardship for disciples who are already believers, rather than the terms for getting saved.

notes.meaning: Clinging to this earthly life at all costs leads to the loss of eternal life, but giving up one's life for Jesus leads to true life. If a person could win the wealth and pleasure of the whole world, it would do no good if their very soul is destroyed. Our souls are our true selves, and no earthly treasure can make up for being cast away from God forever.

Anyone who feels embarrassed by Jesus or His teachings in front of others will face fearful judgment. When the Lord returns in all His divine glory, surrounded by the holy angels, He will refuse to claim that cowardly person as His own. Knowing the great majesty of Christ's return frees His followers from the fear of human disapproval.

Jesus assures the crowd that some people standing there would see the power of God's rule before they died. Many saw this begin just days later at the transfiguration, while others witnessed it through the resurrection and the spread of the church at Pentecost. God proved that His kingdom was breaking into the world during their very lifetime.

differ.view: This promise was fulfilled when Jesus rose and ascended to receive the kingdom from the Father, beginning His reign through the church.
The full earthly kingdom promised in the Old Testament was postponed, so this verse gave only a temporary preview on the mountain.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that Jesus expected the end of the world to happen in that generation and was mistaken.

notes.meaning: About a week after talking about His coming death, Jesus took Peter, John, and James up a mountain to pray. He regularly went off into quiet places to speak with His Father. This special mountain prayer was meant to strengthen the three disciples and build their confidence after hearing hard news about Christ's cross.

While Jesus was praying, the look of His face changed, and His clothing shone with a blinding white light. Luke avoids pagan words for changing shape and simply describes how Christ's heavenly splendor flashed like lightning from within Him. For a brief moment, the Lord revealed His true glory as King of heaven instead of hiding it in humble human weakness.

Moses and Elijah, two great figures from the Old Testament, suddenly appeared and talked with Jesus. Moses represents God's Law and Elijah represents the Prophets, showing that all the ancient Scriptures point directly to Christ. Luke calls them men, reminding us that even the greatest ancient heroes are merely servants while Jesus is the Master.

These two prophets appeared in heavenly glory and spoke with Jesus about His approaching death in Jerusalem. The word for His departure recalls the Exodus, when God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt. By dying and rising again, Jesus was about to accomplish a far greater rescue from sin and death for all His people.

Peter and the other two apostles were overcome with sleep during the long night of prayer, but when they woke up, they saw Jesus in radiant light with the two prophets. Their natural weakness kept them drowsy, just as it would later in the garden of Gethsemane. Yet God woke them in time so they could be reliable eyewitnesses of His royal majesty.

As Moses and Elijah started to leave, Peter blurted out that it was wonderful to be there and offered to build three temporary shelters. He spoke foolishly because he wanted to keep this heavenly joy right on earth. In trying to hold onto the mountaintop, Peter did not realize he was suggesting a way to bypass the suffering of the cross.

A bright cloud rolled in and covered them while Peter was still talking, filling the disciples with holy dread. This was the same divine cloud that once rested over the tabernacle and temple in the Old Testament to show God's personal presence. Entering into God's pure holiness naturally produces awe in sinful people.

God the Father spoke from the cloud, announcing that Jesus is His chosen Son and commanding the disciples to listen to Him. Moses and Elijah were great teachers, but Jesus carries the ultimate authority from God. Believers must submit to His words above all else, even when He speaks about suffering and the cross.

When the heavenly voice ended, the cloud lifted and Jesus was left standing entirely by Himself. The prophets had finished their task and faded away, leaving only Christ as the true Savior. The three disciples kept this sight secret for a time, waiting until after the resurrection when people could fully understand what it meant.

The following day, Jesus and the three apostles walked down the mountain and were immediately met by a large crowd. Leaving behind the peaceful glory of the heights, the Lord returned to the messy troubles of human life. He showed that holy mountaintop experiences must lead back to serving people in need.

A desperate father called out from the crowd, begging Jesus to have mercy on his only son. A single compassionate look from the Lord can fix the most hopeless situation. The father poured out his deep grief, trusting that Christ cared about the pain in his family.

The father explained that an evil spirit repeatedly attacked the boy, causing sudden screaming, terrible convulsions, and foaming at the mouth. The demon bruised the child severely and gave him very little rest. Satan always seeks to bring misery and ruin wherever he gets a foothold in people's lives.

The father had asked the other nine disciples to cast out the demon, but they were completely unable to do it. Even though Jesus had earlier given them authority over evil spirits, their efforts failed here. They had likely become self-confident, doubted God's power, or neglected real prayer.

Jesus grieved over the twisted unbelief of the people, asking how long He must put up with their lack of faith before calling for the boy. Coming down from the purity of the mountain to such spiritual weakness and confusion weighed heavily on His heart. Yet despite His sorrow over their unbelief, Jesus immediately showed tender mercy and prepared to heal the child.
